Patient demographics:

  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

Vignette:
Amir had grown up with a father whose temper was as unpredictable as it was explosive. He remembered the sound of his mother's pleading, the crash of furniture, and the feeling of being pinned against the wall, unable to move or escape. As a child, he learned to read his father's face like a map, searching for signs of impending danger: the furrowed brow, the clenched jaw, the narrowing eyes. One misstep, one careless word, could trigger a violent outburst. As Amir grew older, he began to develop strategies to avoid these confrontations. He became adept at deflecting arguments, dodging disagreements with his parents and later with friends. In college, he steered clear of discussions that might lead to conflict, opting for solo projects instead of group work. His professors praised his independence, but Amir knew the truth: he was terrified of being caught off guard. But avoidance had its costs. Amir's relationships began to suffer. His wife, Sara, complained that he never wanted to talk about anything meaningful, that he always changed the subject or walked away when she tried to bring up sensitive topics. Amir knew she was right; he just couldn't shake the feeling of being trapped, of being unable to escape if things escalated. Amir's job as an environmental scientist required him to work in teams, but he found himself gravitating towards solo fieldwork, opting for remote sites where he could be alone with his thoughts. He'd sit in the backseat on car rides, always positioning himself near the door, ready to bolt if needed. In meetings, he'd choose seats that allowed him to see everyone's face, searching for signs of hostility or aggression. At home, Amir would often find excuses to leave the room when Sara cried, unable to bear the sound of her tears. He knew it was irrational – she wasn't his father, after all – but the associations ran deep. And when they were out in public, he'd instinctively scan the crowd, studying faces and body language for potential threats. One day, Amir's boss assigned him to lead a team project, requiring him to facilitate group discussions and manage conflicts. The prospect sent Amir into a tailspin of anxiety. He couldn't sleep that night, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios: arguments erupting, people shouting, the feeling of being overwhelmed and trapped. It was then that Amir realized he needed help. The strategies he'd developed as a child were no longer serving him; in fact, they were holding him back. He couldn't keep living like this – constantly on edge, always looking over his shoulder. With Sara's encouragement, Amir made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to learn new ways to navigate the world without being controlled by his fears. As he sat in the waiting room, Amir felt a familiar sense of unease. His back was against the wall, and he could see everyone in the room – but it wasn't enough. He was scared of what might come next, of what the therapist would uncover or what memories might resurface. But for the first time in his life, Amir felt ready to face those fears head-on.
